stem: These cases are invented for practice. Two cases show the same resting ball. First case: a gentle push. Second case: a stronger push, the same way on the same floor. Write one sentence. Pick the case that should change the ball's motion more. Give your reason.
answer: The second case. The stronger push should make the bigger change in the motion. A push can change motion.
steps: picks the second case, the stronger push | says why: a stronger push changes the motion more, or a push changes motion
samples: The second case, because a harder push makes more change than a gentle one. | The first case, because gentle is careful.

stem: These rows are invented for practice. Three dated rows tell where the sun was. In every row the morning sun is low on the left. Noon is high. Afternoon is low on the right. Draw where the sun will be next morning. Tell which rows help you decide.
answer: Low on the left, because in all three rows the morning sun was low on the left. This tests predicting from records, not why the sun moves.
steps: draws the next morning sun low on the left | names the three morning rows as the reason
samples: Low on the left. All three mornings had the sun low on the left. | On the left, because I like the left.

stem: This chart is invented for practice. Five dated days show rainy, sunny, rainy, cloudy, rainy. Count the rainy days. Then write what you will put in the chart for tomorrow.
answer: 3 rainy days. For tomorrow, write the date and the weather you really see. A picture is fine.
steps: counts 3 rainy days | writes tomorrow's date and what is really seen, in words or a picture
samples: 3 rainy days. Tomorrow I write the date and draw what the weather looks like. | 2 days. I write rainy because it was rainy a lot.

stem: (a) A girl pushes a wagon along a path. Draw the arrow for her push. (b) Arrow 1 is longer than arrow 2. What does the longer arrow tell you? (c) Write one question you have about how a swing moves.
answer: (a) A short arrow that starts on the wagon where her hands touch it and points the way the wagon goes. It is not drawn along the whole path. (b) A longer arrow means a stronger push. It does not mean the wagon goes farther. (c) Any question about how a swing starts, stops, turns or comes back.
steps: (a) the arrow starts on the wagon at her hands | (a) it points the way the wagon goes and is short, not drawn along the path | (b) says a longer arrow is a stronger push | (c) asks a question about how a swing moves
samples: (a) A short arrow on the wagon at her hands, pointing forward. (b) A stronger push. (c) Why does the swing stop? | (a) A long arrow drawn along the whole path. (b) The wagon went farther.

stem: A wind table is invented for practice. Monday: north. Tuesday: north. Wednesday: south. Thursday: north. Which way do you expect Friday's wind? Say what you saw and how sure you are.
answer: North, because three of the four days were north. This is a prediction, not a sure thing.
steps: predicts north | gives the repeated entries (three of the four days) as the reason | says it is what they expect, not certain
samples: I think north, because it was north on three of the four days. | North, because Thursday was north.

stem: Invented for practice. Mia tests if a harder flick sends a toy car farther. Write her plan. Say what she changes, keeps the same and watches.
answer: Change: how hard the flick is, gentle or hard. Keep the same: the toy car, the floor and the start line. Watch: how far the car goes.
steps: changes one thing, how hard the flick is | keeps the car, the floor and the start line the same | watches how far the car goes
samples: Change: how hard the flick is. Keep: the car, the floor, the start line. Watch: how far it goes. | Change the car and the flick. Watch if it moves.

stem: Kim rolled her toy truck one time and says she is sure. Should she roll again? Say why.
answer: Yes. She should roll again to see if it happens again. Teacher note: ask 3 to 4 children.
steps: says roll again | gives a reason: to see if it happens again
samples: Yes, roll again to see if the same thing happens. | No, once is enough.

stem: Invented for practice. Two children pull a toy boat with strings from opposite banks. Sam drew two arrows of the same length. The boat moved toward the left bank. Draw the arrows again so they fit.
answer: Two arrows starting on the boat, one pointing left and one pointing right. The left arrow is longer, because the boat moved left.
steps: both arrows start on the boat and point opposite ways | the arrow toward the left bank is longer than the other
samples: Two arrows on the boat, the left one longer than the right one. | Two arrows the same length.

stem: A girl holds a book still against a wall with her hand. Is any force on the book? Say why.
answer: Yes. Her hand pushes the book one way and the wall pushes back the other way. The two pushes cancel. Teacher note: ask 3 to 4 children.
steps: says yes, there is a force on the book | names the hand push and the wall push as balanced
samples: Yes, her hand pushes and the wall pushes back. | No, it is not moving.

stem: Each card is invented for practice. Card 1: a wagon at rest, one arrow pointing left. Card 2: a wagon rolling left, one arrow pointing right. Card 3: a wagon rolling left, one long arrow pointing toward the top of the page. Card 4: a package at rest, two equal arrows from opposite sides. (a) Say what each card shows will happen. (b) Which card has the strongest push? (c) Draw which way gravity points on card 4.
answer: (a) Card 1: the wagon starts moving left. Card 2: the wagon slows down. Card 3: the wagon turns toward the top of the page. Card 4: the package stays still because the pushes cancel. (b) Card 3, the longest arrow. (c) Gravity points down toward the floor.
steps: (a) card 1 starts, card 2 slows, card 3 turns toward the top of the page | (a) card 4 stays still because the pushes cancel | (b) picks the card with the longest arrow | (c) draws gravity pointing down
samples: (a) 1 starts left. 2 slows down. 3 turns to the top. 4 stays, the pushes cancel. (b) Card 3. (c) A down arrow. | (a) Card 4 moves left. (b) The ball that goes farthest.

stem: A plan pushes a block from the left with one finger. Then it pushes from the right with two fingers. It wants to know if direction matters. What should the plan change?
answer: Use the same number of fingers both times and change only the direction.
steps: keeps the number of fingers the same | changes only the direction
samples: Use one finger both times and only change the direction. | It is fine, the direction is different.

stem: The plan pushes a block each way, one time each. What else does it need?
answer: More tries of each way. Repeat each condition, about three times. Teacher note: ask 3 to 4 children.
steps: asks for more tries of each way
samples: It needs more tries of each way. | Nothing, it has both ways.

stem: A group pushes a lunch box on a desk. The pushes come from the left and the right, about equal. Three tries moved it 0 cm, 0 cm and 3 cm. What do the results show?
answer: It mostly stayed. 0 cm means less than 1 cm. The 3 cm try may mean the two hands were not equal.
steps: says it mostly stayed | gives a reason the 3 cm try may differ (the pushes were not exactly equal)
samples: It mostly stayed. The 3 may be because the hands were not equal. | Equal pushes make it move.

stem: The group's three tries on the card are done. What does the group do next?
answer: The group runs it again and keeps all three results. Teacher note: ask 3 to 4 children.
steps: says to run it again | says to keep all three results
samples: Run it again and keep all three. | Erase the 3.

stem: A lantern hangs still from a hook by a rope. Draw the arrows on the lantern.
answer: Two arrows on the lantern, the same length. Gravity pulls it down and the rope pulls it up. They cancel.
steps: draws an arrow down for gravity | draws an arrow up for the rope | the two arrows are the same length | the arrows are on the lantern, not along the rope
samples: Two arrows starting on the lantern, one down and one up, the same length. | Nothing pulls it, it is still. Or one arrow as long as the rope.

stem: A toy hangs and swings. Its record: toward the door, middle, toward the window, middle, toward the door, middle. Where is it at the next turn?
answer: Toward the window.
steps: says toward the window
samples: Toward the window. | Toward the door, it started there.

stem: Another swing's far turns are 15, 14, 14 and 13 cm. Will the next far turn be exactly 15 cm? Say why.
answer: No. The far turns have been getting a little smaller. Teacher note: ask 3 to 4 children.
steps: says no | uses the smaller turns as the reason
samples: No, they have been getting a little smaller. | Yes, it always goes the same.

stem: A rocking toy has a record. Left turn, center, right turn, center. Left turn, center, right turn, center. Left turn, center, right turn. What comes next? Say what you saw.
answer: Center. Every right turn in the record was followed by center.
steps: says center | names the earlier right turns followed by center as the evidence
samples: Center, because each right turn was followed by center. | Right turn, it stays where it is now. Or: Left, I like left.

stem: A can rolls back and forth in a curved skate dip. Record: left side 9 cm up, bottom, right side 8 cm up, bottom, left side 7 cm up. Where is the can next?
answer: The bottom.
steps: says the bottom
samples: The bottom. | The right side again, it stays there.

stem: Look at the can's record on the card. Will its next left turn be exactly as high as the last left turn? Say why.
answer: No. It will be a little lower. Each turn has been a bit smaller. Teacher note: ask 3 to 4 children.
steps: says no, a little lower | uses the turns getting smaller as the reason
samples: No, a little lower, because each turn was a bit smaller. | Yes, it always goes the same.

stem: A hanging bucket on a porch hook is made shorter. Pat says it will stay on the left because it started there. Its record shows left, center, right, center. Was Pat right? Say what you think now.
answer: No. It still goes left, center, right, center.
steps: says Pat was not right | gives the record order left, center, right, center
samples: No, it went left, center, right, center. | Yes, it started on the left.

stem: Pat saw the bucket go left, center, right, center one time and says it always works. What should Pat do?
answer: Run it again and compare. Teacher note: ask 3 to 4 children.
steps: says to run it again and compare
samples: Pat should run it again and compare. | Nothing, it worked.

stem: Invented for practice. A cart rests at the bottom of a U-shaped track. Two equal arrows push it from opposite sides. Does it move? Say why.
answer: No. The two equal pushes cancel.
steps: says it does not move | says the equal opposite pushes cancel
samples: No, the two equal pushes cancel. | Yes, two pushes start it.

stem: Invented for practice. A cart is let go from a raised end of a track. Its record: start, middle, far end, middle, start, middle, far end, middle. Where is it next? Say why.
answer: Start (a little lower is fine), because the order has repeated. Teacher note: ask 3 to 4 children.
steps: says start | gives the repeated order as the reason
samples: Start, because the order start, middle, far end, middle happened twice. | The far end, it stays there.

stem: Card 3 is invented for practice. The cart passes the bottom moving right. A new long arrow pointing right is drawn on it. No one has watched since. What could the new arrow change? Can the old record say where it goes next?
answer: The new push could change its speed or its direction. No. Nothing new has been seen, so the old record cannot say.
steps: says the new push could change its speed or direction | says the old record cannot say where it goes next | gives a reason: the conditions changed and nothing new was seen
samples: It could change how fast it goes. The old record cannot tell us because we have not watched since the arrow. | Yes, the old pattern still tells us. Or: the long arrow means it goes far.

stem: Invented for practice. A book rests on a desk. Two about equal pushes touch it from opposite sides. Draw the two arrows. Will it move?
answer: Two arrows on the book pointing toward it from opposite sides, the same length. The pushes cancel, so the book stays still. Unscored.
steps: two arrows on the book, opposite, the same length | says the pushes cancel and the book stays still
samples: Two equal arrows toward the box from each side. The box stays because the pushes cancel. | One arrow only, or: the box moves.

stem: Invented for practice. A bead swings on a string: far left, middle, far right, middle, far left. What comes next? Say why.
answer: Middle, because the order far left, middle, far right, middle has repeated. Unscored. Teacher note: ask 3 to 4 children.
steps: says middle | gives the earlier order as the reason
samples: Middle. After each far side the bead came to the middle. | Far left, because I like left.

stem: Look at today's basket record. Check the order of the turns and the center crossings. Scored from today's work. Write nothing here.
answer: The record shows at least two cycles in the order the child saw, starting with the side really seen first: turning positions left or right with a center crossing between them. A turn too quick to read is left blank. Score 2: 1 for the turns in the order seen, 1 for the center crossings between them.
steps: (1 point) turning positions in the order the child saw, at least two cycles | (1 point) a center crossing recorded between the turns
samples: R C L C R C L C, as seen, with one turn left blank because it was too quick to read. | R R R R, every turn on the side it began.

stem: Look at today's basket record. Check the marked repeating order, the prediction and the evidence. Scored from today's work. Write nothing here.
answer: The repeating order is marked (for example right, center, left, center). The next turning side is opposite the last left or right turn recorded. Two earlier cycles are used as the evidence. Score 4: 1 for the order marked, 1 for the prediction, 2 for evidence linking the record to a repeating motion.
steps: (1 point) marks the repeating order on the record | (1 point) predicts the side opposite the last left or right turn recorded | (2 points) uses two earlier cycles as evidence for the prediction
samples: Order marked. Next is left, because the turns went right, left, right, and that order happened twice. | It stays right, because it started right.

stem: Look at today's sled plan. Check the one change, what stayed the same, and the repeated tries. Scored from today's work. Write nothing here.
answer: The plan changes only one thing, the strength of one push; any single change with everything else kept earns the 2 points. The sled, tray, start line, where the pushes touch and their directions are kept the same. Each way is tried more than once. Score 3: 2 for one change with everything else kept, 1 for repeated tries.
steps: (2 points) names one change (strength expected; any single change counts) and keeps the other conditions the same | (1 point) repeats each condition
samples: I change only the strength. I keep the sled, tray, line and directions. Each way five times, one for each of us. | I change the strength and the tray. One try.

stem: Look at today's sled trials. Check your own marked trial and the readings you wrote. Scored from today's work. Write nothing here.
answer: Two rows, about equal pushes and one stronger push, each with the child's initials and the child's own whole-centimeter reading, written as it happened. An unexpected result is kept, with a retest idea. Score 2: 1 for the child's own marked trial, 1 for the child's own reading of each trial.
steps: (1 point) a trial is marked with the child's initials | (1 point) the child wrote the reading of each trial, in whole centimeters, as it happened
samples: Equal, 1 cm, my initials. Stronger, 9 cm, my initials. | Equal, 0 cm and stronger, 9 cm, copied from the group next door.

stem: Look at today's sled drawing. Check your arrows and your explanation. Scored from today's work. Write nothing here.
answer: Arrows on the sled show the pushes: equal arrows from opposite sides where it stayed, and an arrow that is not cancelled where it moved. The explanation says equal opposite pushes cancel and leave the sled where it was, and a push that is not cancelled can change its motion, and it uses the readings. A child who says hand pushes are only about equal is rewarded. Score 5: 1 for balanced, 1 for unbalanced, 1 for arrows, 2 for evidence.
steps: (1 point) says equal opposite pushes cancel and the sled stays | (1 point) says a push that is not cancelled can change the motion | (1 point) arrows on the sled match the pushes in each condition | (2 points) uses the child's own readings as the evidence
samples: Two equal arrows, it stayed 1 cm: they cancel. One long arrow, it moved 9 cm: not cancelled. | It stayed because no pushes were on it.

stem: Copy card A, B or C. Draw the thing pushed or pulled. Draw the force arrow.
answer: An arrow that starts on the thing pushed or pulled, points the way the push or pull goes, and is longer for a harder push (card B).
steps: the arrow starts on the thing pushed or pulled | the arrow points the way the force goes | a harder push (card B) has the longer arrow
samples: A ball with a short arrow starting on it, pointing right. | A long arrow drawn all along the path the ball rolls.

stem: Draw the washer on its string. Draw the arrows you think make it start, stop and come back. Write what you saw.
answer: A washer on a string with at least one arrow that starts on the washer, and a sentence that names something seen. Any first idea is welcome.
steps: draws the washer on its string | draws at least one arrow that starts on the washer | writes I think ___, because I saw ___ with something that was seen
samples: A washer on a string with an arrow starting on it, pointing to the side. I think a push starts it, because I saw the teacher let go. | A string and washer with no arrow, and no sentence.

stem: Push the ball gently, then harder, from one line. Read each distance. Draw the ball and two arrows.
answer: One ball with two arrows that start on it and point the way it was pushed, the longer arrow for the harder push, and two distances written in whole centimeters.
steps: both arrows start on the ball and point the way it was pushed | the harder push has the longer arrow | each distance is written in whole centimeters
samples: A ball with a short arrow and a longer arrow, both starting on it. Gentle 12 cm. Harder 30 cm. | One long arrow drawn along the path the ball rolled.

stem: Look at the thermometer, the rain jar, the direction card and the sky. Write today's row.
answer: A row with today's date, the temperature to the nearest mark, water or none in the rain jar, the wind direction from the card, and a sky word or picture. Only what was really seen.
steps: writes today's date | writes the temperature to the nearest mark | writes water or none for the rain jar | writes the wind direction from the card | writes a sky word or picture
samples: Date, 8 degrees, none, north, cloudy. | Date, sunny, it will not rain, my guess.

stem: The pond record: sunny, sunny, cloudy, rainy, sunny. The hill record: rainy, cloudy, rainy, rainy, sunny. Which record makes you expect sunny tomorrow? Why?
answer: The pond record, because three of its five days were sunny. This is what we expect, not a sure thing.
steps: picks the pond record | gives the repeated sunny days as the reason | says it is what they expect, not sure
samples: The pond record, because it was sunny on three of the five days. | The hill record, because it ended with sunny.

stem: This test is invented for practice. Rin rolls a marble down a short board. Then Rin rolls a heavy ball down a long board. What did Rin change? How can Rin make it fair?
answer: Rin changed the ball and the board, two things. To make it fair, change only one thing and keep the other the same.
steps: names both changes, the ball and the board | says to change only one thing and keep the rest the same
samples: Rin changed the ball and the board. Use the same ball on both boards. | It is fair, Rin changed the ball.

stem: Do equal pushes from opposite sides change how a box moves? Write what you think and why.
answer: Any prediction that the box will stay or move, with a reason from something seen or felt. A prediction can be wrong; a reason that is only a liking is not enough.
steps: says what the box will do, stay or move | gives a reason from something seen or felt
samples: I think it will stay, because when we pushed from both sides it felt stuck. | I think it will move, because I want it to.

stem: Fill in our plan for the box test. Add your group's practice tries in whole centimeters.
answer: We change how strong one of the two pushes is. We keep the box, tray, start line, where the pushes touch, and both pushes toward the box. We watch where the box ends, in whole centimeters. Three tries of each. One practice try of each, read in whole centimeters.
steps: one change named: how strong one push is | the box, tray, start line and where the pushes touch are kept | watches where the box ends in whole centimeters | three tries of each | a practice try of each in whole centimeters
samples: Change: how strong one push is. Keep: the box, tray, line, where we push. Watch: where the box ends in cm. Three tries of each. Practice: 0 cm and 6 cm. | Change: the box and the push. Watch: if it moves. One try.

stem: Pat puts a box with its edge on the 2 cm mark of a ruler. After a push its edge is on the 9 cm mark. How far did the box move?
answer: 7 cm. The box started at 2 cm and ended at 9 cm, so it moved 9 take away 2.
steps: says the box moved 7 cm | uses the start mark and the end mark, not the end mark alone
samples: 7 cm, because it went from 2 to 9. | 9 cm.

stem: Run the box test. After each try, write where the box ended in whole centimeters.
answer: Six readings in whole centimeters, three for about equal pushes and three for one push stronger, written as they were seen, even if a result is unexpected.
steps: three readings for about equal pushes | three readings for one push stronger | every reading in whole centimeters, as seen
samples: About equal: 0, 0, 0. One stronger: 6, 8, 7. | About equal: 0, 0, 3 changed to 0 to match the plan.

stem: Draw the box and its arrows for both kinds of pushes. Say what you changed. Finish the sentence about the pushes.
answer: We changed how strong one push was. About equal pushes: two arrows of the same length starting on the box. One stronger: one arrow longer. The pushes are balanced when the box stayed, because the ruler read 0 cm.
steps: says the one change, how strong one push was | draws equal arrows starting on the box where the box stayed | draws a longer arrow where one push was stronger | the sentence cites the ruler reading
samples: We changed how hard one push was. Equal arrows when it stayed, a longer arrow when it moved. The pushes are equal because the box stayed at 0 cm. | We changed the box. One long arrow along the path. The pushes are strong.

stem: A ball rolls toward the far end of the tray. A push comes from behind it. Draw the ball and the arrow. What does the ball do?
answer: An arrow that starts on the ball and points toward the far end, the way the ball is rolling. The ball speeds up.
steps: the arrow starts on the ball | the arrow points toward the far end | says the ball speeds up
samples: An arrow on the ball pointing to the far end. It speeds up. | An arrow pointing back toward me. It stops.

stem: A box rests on a tray. Gravity pulls it down. The tray pushes it up. Draw both arrows on the box.
answer: One arrow pointing down and one arrow pointing up, both starting on the box and the same length. The two cancel, so the box stays still.
steps: one arrow down and one arrow up | both start on the box | the two arrows are the same length
samples: A down arrow and an up arrow, the same length, both on the box. | One arrow down only.

stem: Read the thermometer, the rain jar, the direction card and the sky. Write the row for today.
answer: A row with today's date, the temperature to the nearest mark, water or none in the rain jar, the wind direction from the card, and a sky word or picture. Only what was really seen.
steps: writes today's date | writes the temperature to the nearest mark | writes water or none for the rain jar | writes the wind direction from the card | writes a sky word or picture
samples: 5 Nov, 4 degrees, none, west, cloudy. | Nice day, I like it.

stem: Each card is invented for practice. The first card: a toy car at rest, one arrow pointing right. The second card: a toy car moving right, one arrow pointing left. The third card: a toy car moving right, one arrow pointing to the side. Say what each card shows will happen.
answer: First card: the car starts moving right. Second card: the car slows down. Third card: the car turns to the side.
steps: first card starts | second card slows | third card turns to the side
samples: First starts, second slows, third turns. | The first stays, because it is resting.

stem: Choose two practice cards. For each, write what the object does, which arrow is stronger and where gravity points.
answer: For each chosen card: what it does (starts, slows, speeds up or turns), the longer arrow named as the stronger push, and gravity pointing down toward the floor.
steps: says what the object does for both cards | names the longer arrow as stronger | says gravity points down
samples: Puck: it starts. The one arrow is the push. Gravity points down. | The longest arrow goes farthest, and gravity points up.

stem: Write today's row in your weather table. Write the date, the temperature, rain or snow, the wind and the sky.
answer: A row with today's date, the temperature to the nearest mark, water or none in the rain jar, the wind direction from the card, and a sky word or picture. Only what was really seen.
steps: writes today's date | writes the temperature to the nearest mark | writes water or none for the rain jar | writes the wind direction from the card | writes a sky word or picture
samples: 9 Nov, 6 degrees, none, south, cloudy. | Nice day, I like it.

stem: This test is invented for practice. Mo slides a book on a desk with a gentle push. Then Mo slides a book on the carpet with a hard push. What did Mo change? How can Mo make it fair?
answer: Mo changed two things, the floor and the push. To make it fair, change only one thing and keep the other the same.
steps: names both changes, the floor and the push | says to change only one thing and keep the rest the same
samples: Mo changed the floor and the push. Use the same floor both times. | It is fair, Mo changed the push.

stem: An invented crate sits on a smooth floor. In the first case, one child pushes it from the front. Another child pushes from the back. In the second case, two children both push it from the front. Every push is about equal in strength. Which feature of the push changed? Which two features stayed the same?
answer: Which way the pushes go changed: front and back, then both from the front. The number of pushes, two, and how strong they are, about equal, stayed the same.
steps: the first case has two pushes, about equal, from opposite sides | the second case has two pushes, about equal, both from the front | the number of pushes and how strong they are are the same in both | only which way the pushes go changed
samples: Which way changed. The number and the strength stayed the same. | The crate changed, and so did the floor.

stem: Fill in your group's plan for the push test. Choose one change and say what you keep.
answer: We change which way the pushes go. We keep the box, the tray, the start line, two pushes about equal in strength and where they touch. We watch where the box ends, in whole centimeters. Three tries of each way. The unbalanced pair is named, both from the front or one from the front and one from the side.
steps: one change named: which way the pushes go | keeps the box, tray, start line, number of pushes and strength | watches where the box ends in whole centimeters | three tries of each way | names the unbalanced pair
samples: We change the direction. We keep the box, the tray, the line and two equal pushes. We watch where the box ends in cm. Three tries each. Unbalanced: both from the front. | We change the box and the push. We watch if it moves. One try.

stem: Draw the box and the arrows for each pair of pushes your group will try. Write what you think the box will do, and why.
answer: Balanced pair: two arrows of the same length from opposite sides, both starting on the box. Unbalanced pair: arrows drawn the way the group will push. A prediction for each pair, with a reason from the earlier box tests, such as: equal pushes cancel, so the box should stay.
steps: balanced pair drawn as two arrows of the same length from opposite sides, on the box | unbalanced pair drawn the way the group chose | says what the box will do for each pair | gives a reason from earlier tests
samples: Balanced: two same arrows on the box, front and back. Unbalanced: two arrows from the front. I think the balanced box stays and the unbalanced box moves, because equal pushes cancel. | I think it will move because I like it.

stem: Read the plan of another group. Tick what you find. Write one question for them.
answer: Ticks only for what the plan really shows: one change, the rest kept, three tries of each way. One question about the plan, such as how they will keep the two pushes about equal.
steps: ticks match what the plan really shows | writes one question about the plan
samples: Ticks: one change, the rest kept, three tries. Question: How will you keep the pushes about equal? | It is good.

stem: Write your own plan for the push test. Say what you change, what you keep and how many tries.
answer: I change which way the pushes go. I keep the box, the tray, the start line, two pushes about equal in strength and where they touch. I try each way three times.
steps: one change named: which way the pushes go | keeps the box, tray, start line, number and strength of pushes | says how many tries of each way
samples: I change the direction. I keep the box, the tray, the line and two equal pushes. Three tries each way. | I change the box and the push. One try.

stem: Run the push test. After each try, write who pushed and where the box ended in whole centimeters.
answer: Six rows, three for balanced pushes and three for unbalanced pushes. Every try has the pusher's initials and a reading in whole centimeters, written as it was seen, even if a result is unexpected.
steps: three readings for balanced pushes | three readings for unbalanced pushes | initials on every try | every reading in whole centimeters, as seen
samples: Balanced: 0, 1, 0. Unbalanced: 8, 6, 9. Initials on every row. | Balanced: 1, 0, 1 changed to 0, 0, 0 to match the plan.

stem: Draw the box and its arrows for both kinds of pushes. Write what stayed or moved, and why. Use balanced or unbalanced and a number from your table.
answer: Balanced pair: two arrows of the same length from opposite sides, starting on the box. Unbalanced pair: the arrows as your group pushed. Two sentences, such as: The box stayed, about 1 cm, because the pushes were balanced. It moved 8 cm because the pushes were unbalanced.
steps: arrows for the balanced pair match what was seen | arrows for the unbalanced pair match what was seen | says what stayed or moved | says why, with balanced or unbalanced and a centimeter reading
samples: Balanced: same arrows, front and back, on the box. Unbalanced: two arrows from the front. The box stayed, 1 cm, because the pushes were balanced. It moved 7 cm because they were unbalanced. | The box moved because it wanted to.

stem: Read the note on your day 7 record. Revise it in a second color. Keep your first numbers and initials.
answer: The first readings and initials are still there. Every change is in a second color. At least one change answers the written note, to the plan, the arrows or the sentences.
steps: first readings and initials kept | changes written in a second color | at least one change answers the written note
samples: My numbers stay. In green I added: we kept the pushes about equal. | I rubbed out my 3 and wrote 0.

stem: Item 1. Use the marigold and duckling card. Explain the water effect. Explain the learned response. Explain the combined influences. Pick each observation and give its reason.
answer: Marigolds given enough water grew 12 and 13 cm and those given too little grew 6 and 7, with light, age, soil and spacing fixed, so water had an effect. The ducklings ignored the bell and, after the bell sounded before each feeding, came to it, so they learned it. The short and tall families keep their pattern under matched water, and less water lowers both, so family and water both shape height.
steps: a water claim from the matched marigolds | a learning claim from the before and after ducklings | the family pattern and the water both named for height | reasoning that both can shape one feature, not one cause for every difference
samples: The watered marigolds were 12 and 13 and the dry ones 6 and 7, and the rest was fixed, so water mattered. The ducklings ignored the bell first and came after the feedings, so they learned it. Height comes from the family and the water. | All the height differences are inherited. The ducklings inherited knowing the bell.

stem: Reread your explanation. Mark your claim, your evidence and your reason.

stem: Item 2. Draw a model for zinnia Z and one for lady beetle L. Show birth, growth, reproduction and death in each.
answer: Z: seed (day 0), seedling (5), flowering adult (50), dried flower head (70), dead (95); the record shows no reproduction for Z, so its reproduction box is dotted or blank and marked not in this record. L: egg (0), larva (4), pupa (18), adult (25), adult lays eggs (35), dead (90). The beetle model shows birth, growth, reproduction and death.
steps: the plant model has birth and growth and death from the record, and a dotted or blank reproduction box marked not in this record | the animal model has all four, with eggs on day 35 | stages are in the order of the dated record

stem: Say what is the same. Say what differs in stages and timing. Predict what follows a new zinnia seed that begins to grow.
answer: The same: both are born, grow and die, and the beetle also reproduces (eggs on day 35). What differs: the beetle has a pupa and the zinnia has none, and seed to seedling took 5 days while egg to larva took 4. The zinnia record shows no new seeds yet. A new zinnia seed that begins to grow is a seedling after 5 days.
steps: names what is the same: born, grow and die; the beetle laid eggs on day 35 and the zinnia record shows no new seeds yet | names a difference in stages and one in timing | predicts a seedling after 5 days from the supplied timing
samples: Both are born, grow and die. The beetle laid eggs on day 35; the zinnia record shows no new seeds yet. Only the beetle has a pupa. Seed to seedling took 5 days, so a seedling comes after 5 days. | Zinnias and beetles are the same, so I cannot predict.

stem: Second card. Revise your models in a second color. Join Z to the new individuals. Say what the record shows.

steps: adds the seeds in the opened flower head | an arrow from the adult to the new individual, not back to Z | says the seed that begins to grow is the new plant
samples: The head held seeds on day 70. I drew an arrow from Z to a seed that grew into a seedling on day 80. | The same zinnia starts again after it dies. The seeds in the head show it reproduced.

stem: Reread your models. Tick each stage that matches a day in the record.

answer: A labeled table in order spring, summer, autumn, winter with temperatures 16, 26, 32 and 20 degrees Celsius, rainy or snowy days 6, 8, 2 and 4, and usual winds north, north, west and east.
steps: has the four seasons in order | has all three measures | labels each row and column
samples: Spring 16, 6 days, north. Summer 26, 8 days, north. Autumn 32, 2 days, west. Winter 20, 4 days, east. | Winter is cold.

stem: Graph the days with rain or snow. Choose a scale. Label both sides.
answer: Bars at 6, 8, 2 and 4 days with a stated scale that is used, and both sides labeled.
steps: bars at 6, 8, 2 and 4 | the scale is stated and used | both sides are labeled
samples: Bars of 3, 4, 1 and 2 squares, each square 2 days, labeled. | Six squares for 6 days, though the side counts by 2.

stem: Use all three measures. Write what to expect in a season. Say how sure you are.
answer: Summer is usually warmer and wetter than winter in these records, with different usual winds. It is likely and not a guarantee.
steps: uses temperature, rain and wind | says usually or likely | says it is not a guarantee
samples: Summer is usually warmer and wetter than winter, and the winds differ. One day can still differ. | One rainy day means winter is always wet.

stem: Use both cards. Say what M and N are usually like.
answer: M is warm throughout the year and usually has 14 to 26 rainy July days. N has cold winters and mild summers and usually 1 to 9 rainy July days.
steps: uses the atlas card for M and N | uses the station card for M and N
samples: The atlas says M is warm all year, and the station gives 14 to 26 rainy July days. N has cold winters, mild summers and 1 to 9 days. | M is warm all year.

stem: Compare the ranges of M and N in July.
answer: M has more rainy July days than N: 14 to 26 against 1 to 9. N has the greater swing between winter and summer.
steps: compares both ranges with numbers | says which is wetter
samples: M is wetter in July, 14 to 26 days against 1 to 9. | They are the same.

stem: Show how the years change. Say which card each claim comes from.
answer: The selected years change: M had 15, 23 and 19 rainy July days and N had 3, 8 and 5. This is from the station card. Neither place promises tomorrow.
steps: uses the selected years | names the card | does not take one year as the climate
samples: The station card shows M with 15, 23 and 19 and N with 3, 8 and 5, so the years change. | This July is the whole climate of M.

stem: Wind screen. Draw the arrows for the wind, the screen and the markers.
answer: The windstorm, the screen, then fewer markers moved. The wind still blows.
steps: names the wind as the hazard | names the screen as the design | names fewer markers moved as the harm lessened | says the wind still blows
samples: Wind, screen, fewer markers blown away. The wind still blows. | Wind, screen, no wind.

stem: Check the goal and the limit. Use the counts and the cost.
answer: Goal: at least 7 of 9 markers stay. With the screen 7, 8 and 7, so the goal is met; without it 2, 3 and 2. Cost: 12 tokens, within the limit of 13.
steps: uses the counts with and without | checks the cost against 13
samples: With: 7, 8 and 7, goal met. Without: 2, 3 and 2. Cost 12, within 13. | Any cost is fine if it works.

stem: Write a merit claim for the wind screen.
answer: The screen has merit: it meets the goal in all three trials within the cost. It changes how much wind reaches the markers, so less is displaced.
steps: claims merit | uses the goal and the cost | ties the wind to fewer markers moved
samples: I think the screen has merit because 7, 8 and 7 markers stayed for 12 tokens, so fewer markers move. | The screen stops the windstorm.

stem: Say what the trials cannot show.
answer: Stronger winds were not tested, and the model does not show a real waiting area.
steps: names one thing not tested | does not say real places are safe
samples: The record does not show stronger winds. | It will protect every real waiting area.

stem: Reread each statement. Put a tick only where a card or table backs it.
answer: Each statement is ticked only where a record on the card backs it.
steps: reads each statement against a record | ticks only what a record backs
samples: Each statement checked against a record. | All ticked without looking.

stem: Look at your returned work. Mark one component to work on.
answer: One component is marked: displays, evidence spans, source links or design reasoning.
steps: reads the feedback | marks one component
samples: Marked: source links. | Marks every component.

stem: Group 1, displays. Say how many marks 14 days need when each mark is 2 days.
answer: Seven marks. Each mark is 2 days, so 14 days need 7 marks.
steps: reads the key | divides by the scale
samples: 7 marks, because each mark is 2 days. | 14 marks, one for each day.

stem: Group 2, evidence spans. Lay one odd day beside a season. Say what the range shows.
answer: One odd day is not the season; the usual comes from many days. One year is not the climate; the range over many years is.
steps: puts the odd day beside the records | says many days or years set the usual
samples: One stormy day is not a stormy season, and one year sits inside the range. | The season is stormy because one day was.

stem: Group 3, source links. Join a detail from each card in one sentence.
answer: A sentence that joins the atlas card and the station card: warm all year and rain in only 3 months.
steps: uses the atlas card | uses the station card
samples: Region Y is warm all year, and it rains in only 3 months. | Region Y is dry.

stem: Group 4, design reasoning. Fix one claim: say what the design lessens, the limit, and what is untested.
answer: The design lessens what the hazard does; the hazard still happens. Check the limit box first. Name one condition not tested.
steps: says the hazard still happens | checks the limit | names one condition not tested
samples: The shelter lessens what the wind does to the markers. It is within the limit. Stronger wind was not tested. | The shelter stops the storm.

stem: Read the thermometer to the nearest mark. Write the weather record.
answer: The date, the temperature to the nearest mark (below zero said in words), rain or snow, the wind direction and the sky.
steps: writes the date | reads the temperature to the nearest mark, or says below zero | gives rain or snow, the wind direction and the sky
samples: 17 Mar, 8 degrees, rain, south, gray. | Wet.

stem: Invented for practice. A cork block rests on a tray. You will compare two equal pushes from opposite sides with one stronger push. Write what you change, what you keep the same and what you watch. How many tries of each way?
answer: Change: the pushes (two equal pushes from opposite sides, or one stronger push). Keep the same: the block, the tray, the start line and where the hands touch. Watch: how far the block moves, in whole centimeters. Three tries of each way.
steps: changes only the pushes | keeps the block, tray and start line the same | watches the distance in whole centimeters | says about three tries of each way
samples: I change the pushes. I keep the block, tray and start line the same. I watch how far it moves in centimeters. Three tries of each way. | I push the block hard, then I use a lighter block with a soft push. One try each.

stem: Make your own trial at the station. Write your initials. Write each way you pushed. Write what the block did. Write each reading in whole centimeters.
answer: Your initials, both ways you pushed (two equal pushes; one stronger push), what the block did each time (stayed, or moved a way) and each reading in whole centimeters. 0 cm means less than 1 cm.
steps: initials mark the child's own trial | names each way pushed | says what the block did each time | reads each distance to the whole centimeter
samples: J.R. Two equal pushes: it stayed, 0 cm. One stronger push: it slid to the back, 9 cm. | I pushed it and it went.

stem: Draw the force arrows on the block for each way. Say why the block stayed still or moved.
answer: Two equal arrows start on the block and point in from opposite sides. They cancel, so the block stays still. One longer arrow on the block is not cancelled, so the block moves the way the arrow points. Every arrow starts on the block; none runs along the path.
steps: equal arrows from opposite sides on the block that stayed | says equal arrows cancel | a longer arrow on the block that moved, and why it is not cancelled | every arrow starts on the block and none runs along the path
samples: Two equal arrows on the block cancel, so it stays still. One long arrow points the way it slid. | No arrows on the block that stayed, since nothing pushed it.

stem: Look at the weight card. Write the height of the weight at turns 1 to 6.
answer: Turn 1: 14 cm. Turn 2: 10 cm. Turn 3: 6 cm. Turn 4: 10 cm. Turn 5: 13 cm. Turn 6: 10 cm.
steps: reads each picture against the ruler beside it | writes six heights in order | gives whole centimeters
samples: 14, 10, 6, 10, 13, 10. | High, middle, low, middle, high, middle.

stem: Where will the weight be at turn 7 and at turn 8? Say what you saw that tells you.
answer: Turn 7: low, a little higher than 6 cm, about 7 cm. Turn 8: the middle, about 10 cm. The order high, middle, low, middle has repeated, and each far turn has been a little closer to the middle.
steps: turn 7 is the low turn | turn 8 is the middle | says the order repeated | says the far turns get a little closer to the middle
samples: Turn 7 is low, about 7 cm. Turn 8 is about 10 cm. The order repeats and the far turns get closer to the middle. | Turn 7 is the middle again, the same as turn 6.

stem: Read board 1. One claim does not fit the records. Say which one. Fix it with a record.
answer: Claim A does not fit. At 2 cm and 6 cm the ball leaned and nothing touched it, so a pull can cross a gap. Fixed claim: a rubbed comb pulls the ball across a gap, and a bigger gap gives a smaller lean.
steps: picks claim A | cites record 1 or 2, a lean with a gap and nothing touching | says a pull can cross a gap
samples: Claim A. In record 1 the ball leaned 3 cm and the comb did not touch it. A pull can cross a gap. | Claim C, because at 10 cm there was no lean, so there was no pull.

stem: Write one question about board 1 that you can test. Say what you would change.
answer: A question such as: Does a bigger gap make the ball lean less? Change only the gap.
steps: asks about one thing that changes the lean | says the one thing changed
samples: Does the ball lean less at a bigger gap? I change the gap and keep the comb the same. | Which comb is the best?

stem: Read board 2. One claim does not fit the records. Say which one. Fix it with a record.
answer: Claim E does not fit. A steel washer leans toward the magnet, but a brass washer does not lean. Fixed claim: a magnet pulls steel, and it does not pull brass.
steps: picks claim E | cites the brass washer with no lean | says the kind of metal matters
samples: Claim E. The brass washer did not lean, but the steel washer did. | Claim E is right, because both washers are metal.

stem: Draw the arrow on the hung magnet for record 1 and for record 2. Say what turning the second magnet changes.
answer: Record 1: the arrow starts on the hung magnet and points away from the second magnet, a push. Record 2: it points toward the second magnet, a pull. Turning the second magnet around changes a push to a pull.
steps: record 1 arrow starts on the hung magnet and points away | record 2 arrow points toward the second magnet | says turning changes a push to a pull
samples: Record 1: the arrow points away, a push. Record 2: it points toward, a pull. Turning the magnet swaps push and pull. | One arrow drawn along the whole swing of the magnet.

stem: Use your question. Write what you change, what you keep the same and what you watch.
answer: The question and its test: one thing changed, everything else kept the same, one thing watched in whole centimeters.
steps: names one thing changed | names what is kept the same | names what is watched
samples: I change the gap. I keep the magnets and the washer the same. I watch the lean in centimeters. | I change the gap and the magnet together.

stem: Fill in today's weather row. Write the date, temperature, rain jar, wind and sky.
answer: Today's row with the date, the temperature to the nearest mark, the rain jar reading or none, the wind direction and the sky.
steps: writes today's row from what was seen | writes the temperature and the rain jar reading or none
samples: 19 Nov, 4 degrees, none, north, cloudy. | Cold.

stem: Find the slip on your note. Fix it in a second color on a repair card.
answer: One slip is fixed in a second color. The first answer is kept, with the initials beside it.
steps: fixes one slip the note names | uses a second color | keeps the first answer and initials it
samples: I drew the arrow on the block in green and kept the first one. | The first answer is rubbed out.

stem: Invented for practice. Jo pushes a drawer that slides easily, from the front. Kim pushes it from the back, exactly as hard. Draw the arrows on the drawer. Does it move? Say why.
answer: Two equal arrows on the drawer, one from the front and one from the back. No. Equal pushes from opposite sides cancel, so the drawer stays still.
steps: two equal arrows on the drawer from opposite sides | says it does not move, because equal pushes cancel
samples: Two equal arrows on the drawer. It stays still because the pushes cancel. | No arrows. It stays because nothing pushes it.

stem: A feeder flap must stay shut in the wind. You have two magnets and tape. Who needs what?
answer: The birds and the people who fill the feeder need the flap to stay shut so the wind cannot blow the flap open and spill the seed. Teacher note: ask 3 to 4 children.
steps: says who needs what so that
samples: People who fill the feeder need the flap shut so that the seed stays dry. | Two magnets and tape.

stem: A feeder flap must stay shut in the wind. You have two magnets and tape. Say one criterion you can check.
answer: It stays shut in a strong puff of wind. Teacher note: ask 3 to 4 children.
steps: says one criterion that can be checked
samples: It stays shut when I blow on it. | It is a good flap.

stem: Invented for practice. A seesaw end goes up, level, down, level, up, level. Its up turns were 40 cm, then 36 cm. Where is it next? Why?
answer: Down. The order up, level, down, level repeats, so down comes after level. The up turns are also getting a little lower.
steps: says down is next | says the order repeats, so down comes after level | (extra, not needed) the up turns got a little lower
samples: Down. The order up, level, down, level repeats, and level was last. | Level, because it was level last.

stem: Invented for practice. A magnet is held near a hanging steel washer. Write one question you can test about the gap. Say what you change.
answer: A question such as: Does the washer lean less at a bigger gap? Change only the gap. Keep the magnet and the washer the same.
steps: a question about the gap | says the one thing changed | says what stays the same
samples: Does the washer lean less at a bigger gap? I change the gap only. | Which magnet is strongest?

stem: Look at the cosmos card and the grasshopper card. Draw each life as stages in order, with arrows. Show birth, growth, having young and death.
answer: Plant: seed, seedling, flowering adult, seed heads with new seeds, dead plant. Animal: egg, young hopper, winged adult, eggs laid, dead adult. Each model shows birth, growth, having young and death, and the arrows go from the adult to the new young. Score 2.
steps: (1 point) the plant model has birth, growth, having young and death in order | (1 point) the animal model has birth, growth, having young and death in order
samples: Cosmos: seed, seedling, flower, seeds, dead. Grasshopper: egg, young hopper, adult, eggs, dead. | Cosmos: seed, flower, dead. Grasshopper: adult only.

stem: Say one way the two lives are alike. Say one way they differ. Eggs are laid on day 70. When will they hatch?
answer: Alike: both start small, grow, make young and die. Differ: the plant starts as a seed and the grasshopper as an egg, and their times differ. The egg stage on the card lasted 12 days, so eggs laid on day 70 hatch about day 82.
steps: names one way alike | names one way they differ | says about day 82, from the 12 days the egg stage lasted
samples: Both grow and make young. The plant starts as a seed and the grasshopper as an egg. About day 82, because eggs took 12 days. | The two lives are the same, stage for stage.

stem: Sam drew an arrow from the dead grasshopper back to the young hopper. Fix Sam's model. Use the eggs laid on day 70.
answer: The arrow goes from the adult to the eggs it laid on day 70, and the eggs hatch into new young hoppers.
steps: moves the arrow from the dead adult to the eggs laid on day 70 | the eggs hatch into new young
samples: The arrow goes from the adult to its eggs on day 70, and the eggs hatch into new hoppers. | The adult turns back into a young hopper.

stem: Look at the foxglove card. Name one trait the seedlings share with their parents. Give the evidence.
answer: The seedlings have oval, soft-haired leaves, like both parents; either oval leaves or soft, hairy leaves is right.
steps: names oval leaves or soft, hairy leaves | says the parents and the seedlings both have them
samples: Soft, hairy leaves. The parents have them and so do the seedlings. | They are not like their parents, because their heights are different.

stem: Name one trait that differs among the foxglove seedlings. Give the numbers. Are they a different kind?
answer: Height differs: 8, 11, 9 and 14 cm. No. They are all foxgloves, one kind, with a trait that varies.
steps: names height | gives the heights 8, 11, 9 and 14 | says they are still one kind
samples: Height. 8, 11, 9 and 14 cm. They are still all foxgloves. | The 14 cm one is a different kind of plant.

stem: Look at the wren card. Name one trait the chicks share with their parents. Give the evidence.
answer: The chicks have speckled chests and curved tails, like both parents.
steps: names speckled chests or curved tails | says the parents and the chicks both have them
samples: Speckled chests. The parents and the chicks both have them. | The chicks are different weights, so they are not wrens.

stem: Name one trait that differs among the wren chicks. Give the numbers. Are they a different kind?
answer: Weight differs: 12, 14, 13, 15 and 13 g. No. They are all wrens, one kind, with a trait that varies.
steps: names weight | gives the weights 12, 14, 13, 15 and 13 | says they are still one kind
samples: Weight. 12, 14, 13, 15 and 13 g. They are all wrens. | The heaviest chick is another kind of bird.

stem: Panel 1, color. What shaped the chicks' color? Write a claim, the data and a because.
answer: Claim: the food shaped the color. Data: Zoo A chicks fed brine shrimp are pink; Zoo B chicks fed pale grain are pale gray. Because: the chicks came from the same kind of flock and only the food differed.
steps: a claim that the food shaped the color | data from both zoos | a because that the food was the difference
samples: I think the food shaped the color, because Zoo A chicks ate shrimp and are pink, and Zoo B chicks ate grain and are gray. | Pink comes from their parents, so food does not matter.

stem: Panel 1, the feeding clap. Is walking to the clap learned or inherited? Write a claim, the data and a because.
answer: Claim: learned. Data: in week 1 no chick walked to the clap; in week 4 the Zoo A chicks did, and the Zoo B chicks, never clapped for, did not. Because: it changed after the keeper taught it with food, and the chicks without teaching did not do it.
steps: says learned | uses the before and after data | says the untaught chicks did not do it
samples: I think it is learned, because no chick came in week 1 and the Zoo A chicks came in week 4. Zoo B chicks never learned it. | It is inherited, because the chicks are flamingos.

stem: Panel 1, legs. Both zoos have long legs. Zoo B legs are shorter. Explain both with the data.
answer: Both groups of chicks have long legs, 64 to 80 cm, like their long-legged parents of about 100 cm, so the family shows. Zoo B chicks, fed less, are about 13 cm shorter than Zoo A chicks, so the food shows too. Both together shape leg length.
steps: the family shows in the long legs of both zoos | the food shows in the difference between the zoos | says both together
samples: The parents have long legs and so do all the chicks. Zoo B chicks ate less and are shorter. Both matter. | Leg length comes only from the parents.

stem: Panel 2, food. Does a flock help flamingos get food? Write a claim, the data and a because.
answer: Claim: yes. Data: a flamingo alone gets 5 bites a minute, a flock of 8 gets 9 and a flock of 200 gets 14. Because: the flock shares the watching, so each bird can keep feeding.
steps: says a flock helps | uses at least two of 5, 9 and 14 | a because that links the flock to more bites, such as shared watching
samples: I think a flock helps get food, because one bird gets 5 bites and a flock of 200 gets 14. | A flock does not help, since one bird can eat alone.

stem: Panel 2, safety. Does a flock help keep flamingos safe? Write a claim, the data and a because.
answer: Claim: yes, it helps. Data: a lone bird sees a fox at 8 steps and a flock sees it at 40 steps. Because: many eyes see danger sooner.
steps: says a flock helps | uses 8 and 40 steps
samples: I think a flock helps keep birds safe, because a flock sees the fox at 40 steps and one bird at 8.

stem: Panel 2, safety. Can a flock promise safety?
answer: No. It cannot promise safety, because a fox may still catch a bird.
steps: says it does not promise safety
samples: No. A fox may still catch a bird. | A flock keeps every bird safe, always.

stem: Panel 2, a dry spell. The lagoon shrinks and the flock walks to the deep end. How does the flock help its members?
answer: The flock walks together to the deep end, so every bird reaches water and no bird is left alone in the dry end. The group moves together through the change.
steps: says the birds go together | says all reach water | says the group helps through the change
samples: The whole flock walks to the deep end together, so the birds reach water. | The lagoon shrinks, so the flock is no help.

stem: Panel 2, jobs. Compare the small flock and the large flock. What jobs do they have?
answer: Small flock of 8: 1 watcher and 7 feeders. Large flock of 200: 20 watchers and 180 feeders. The large flock has more watchers and more feeders, so more eyes watch while most birds feed.
steps: gives watchers and feeders for both flocks | says the large flock has more watchers
samples: Small: 1 watcher, 7 feeders. Large: 20 watchers, 180 feeders. More watch in the large flock while most feed. | Both flocks have watchers, so they are the same.

stem: Look at your note and your group card. Write the fix in a second color.
answer: One slip is fixed in a second color. The first answer is kept, with the initials beside it.
steps: fixes one slip the note names | uses a second color | keeps the first answer and initials it
samples: I moved the arrow to the eggs, in green, and kept the first one. | The first answer is rubbed out.

stem: Invented for practice. In this model, a pond beetle lives 130 days. On day 120 the adult lays eggs, which hatch in 14 days. Sam draws an arrow from the dead adult back to the young. Fix it.
answer: The arrow goes from the adult to its eggs, and the eggs hatch into new young beetles. The adult does not return as its young.
steps: moves the arrow from the adult to its eggs | says the adult does not return as its own young
samples: The arrow goes from the adult to its eggs. The adult does not come back as its own young. | The adult turns back into a baby beetle.

stem: In this model, a beetle adult lays eggs on day 120, and the eggs hatch in 14 days. When do the eggs hatch?
answer: The eggs hatch on day 134. Teacher note: ask 3 to 4 children.
steps: says day 134
samples: Day 134. | Day 14.

stem: A goose alone looks up 20 times a minute. In a flock of 40, each looks up 6 times. Why does a flock help?
answer: In a flock many eyes watch, so each goose looks up less and eats more. Teacher note: ask 3 to 4 children.
steps: says many eyes watch | says each goose looks up less
samples: Many eyes watch, so each goose looks up less. | Flocks help because geese like company.

stem: A flock of geese looks up less often than a lone goose. Can a flock promise safety?
answer: No. A flock helps, but it cannot promise safety. Teacher note: ask 3 to 4 children.
steps: says it does not promise safety
samples: No. A flock helps but cannot promise safety. | A flock keeps every goose safe.

stem: Invented for practice. Tulip parents have red cup flowers. Four seedlings have red cup flowers. Their leaves are 6, 9, 7 and 10 cm. Name one likeness and one difference. Are they another kind?
answer: Likeness: red cup flowers. Difference: leaf length. No, they are still tulips, one kind.
steps: names red cup flowers | names leaf length | says they are still one kind
samples: Likeness: red cup flowers. Difference: leaf length. They are all tulips. | The 10 cm one is another kind of tulip.

stem: Invented for practice. Cress seeds from one packet grow in light and in shade. Stems are 4 cm in light and 9 cm in shade. What shapes the stems? An otter learns to push a button for fish. Does its new pup know it at birth?
answer: The place shapes the stems, because one packet gave both. The button push is learned, so the pup does not know it at birth.
steps: says the place or the light shaped the stems | says the push is learned | says the pup does not know it at birth
samples: The light shaped the stems, because the seeds were all from one packet. The pup has to learn the button. | The packet decides the stems. The pup knows the button.

stem: Read the dry basin card. The basin is dry now. What do the fish bones and water-plant prints show?

samples: A lake was here long ago, because fish live in water and water plants grow in water. | The basin was always dry, so the bones fell in.

stem: North Cut has fish bones. South Cut has one fish bone and a snail shell. Does this show the whole basin was lake?
answer: No. The two cuts show water at those two places. The rest of the basin needs more places to look at.

samples: No. The cuts show water at those two places only. I would look at more places. | Yes, the whole basin was a lake.

stem: North Cut has a trunk piece 45 cm long. How big was the tree?

samples: At least 45 cm, because the piece may be only part of the trunk. | The tree was 45 cm long.

stem: North Cut has a lower layer and an upper layer. Which came first, the lake or the trees? Say how you know.

samples: The lake came first, because the layers were never moved and lower is older. | The trees came first, because trees are big.

stem: The guide says Gar F lives nowhere now. Is every fish bone at North Cut from an extinct fish? Say how you know.

stem: Mia says the basin was always dry, because this week is hot and dry. Fix her claim with the evidence.

stem: The meadow pool fell from 40 cm to 10 cm. Iris flowers fell from 20 to 4. What does less water do to the flowers?

stem: Draw an arrow from the water to the iris. Draw an arrow from the water to the tadpoles. Label each arrow.
answer: Arrow water to iris, labeled: iris need water to flower. Arrow water to tadpoles, labeled: tadpoles live in the water.

samples: Water to iris: they need water to flower. Water to tadpoles: they live in it. | Iris to water.

stem: Read both goals on the card. Which trials meet them? Give the counts.

stem: The goal is 8 of 10 iris patches in flower. It also needs 6 of 10 net scoops with tadpoles. The limits are 6 tokens and a clear fence line. Which trial meets the goal and fits both limits?

stem: Does Trial A mean every iris and tadpole is saved? Say what the card does not show.
